title: Midterms 2026: Democrats Take Congress
intro: Results, key races and New York, as of Wednesday morning. Race calls are the AP’s unless we say otherwise; leads are leads, not wins.
bannerHeadline: Democrats win the House and Senate: results, key races and New York
bannerDeck: AP calls, uncalled races, ballot measures and what happens next.
ourViewIntro: Donna Daily’s own analysis of what the results mean, setting out more than one side and drawing on the linked reporting.
notes: This is a Donna Daily special edition on the Nov. 3, 2026 US midterm elections. It does not replace the daily edition, and results will keep changing after the “last updated” time above.

Race calls: we only say a candidate “won” when a major news desk has declared it. The AP is our default, and we name CBS News, ABC News or another desk when we rely on theirs. Concessions are reported as concessions. Uncalled races are described as leads.
Seat counts are AP’s as displayed by the Guardian’s results page at 9:10 AM ET on Nov. 4. Ballotpedia’s 1:30 AM tallies differ slightly and are labelled as theirs.

Analysis is split in two: “Our view” pieces are Donna Daily’s own analysis, written to present more than one side; “What columnists are arguing” paraphrases named writers at other outlets, with links to the originals.
provenance: Research pages were opened on Nov. 4, 2026, between about 10:33 and 11:00 AM ET. Individual check times were not logged, so none are shown on the story checks.

AP’s own pages refuse automated access. Where an AP story is cited, its claims were confirmed on a syndicated copy (Boston.com, KLAS, WSOC-TV) or in AP live coverage carried by PBS, and the story check says so.
Some live pages (ABC News) and Florida Politics could only be read through search-index excerpts; this is recorded as an access limit, not as evidence of a broken link.

Photos are from Wikimedia Commons under free licences or the public domain, or are US government works. They were checked on their file pages, cropped to 16:9 and credited under each picture. All are file photos, not pictures of election night.

stories.dateLabel: Called Nov 3–4 · seat counts as of 9:10 AM ET Wed
stories.headline: Democrats win the House and the Senate in a sweeping rebuke of Trump
stories.glance: AP: Democrats win both chambers of Congress
stories.deck: The Associated Press says Democrats won the Senate late Tuesday and the House early Wednesday. AP tallies at 9:10 AM ET: 54 Senate seats to 44, and 228 House seats to 139, with races still being counted.
stories.summary: AP results carried by the Guardian at 9:10 AM ET showed Democrats (counting two independents who caucus with them) at 54 Senate seats to Republicans’ 44, a net gain of seven, with 33 of 35 races called. Alaska and Mississippi were still uncalled. In the House, Democrats had 228 seats to 139, a net gain of 25, with 367 of 435 races called; 218 is a majority. AP said it called Senate control after a flurry of Democratic wins late Tuesday and the House early Wednesday, far faster than 2022, when the Senate call took four days and the House eight. AP’s main story says voters’ frustration over high prices, the Iran war and government corruption drove the result, with Democrats flipping states Trump won by double digits two years ago. Ballotpedia’s own count at 1:30 AM put the floor at 54–44 in the Senate and 231–141 in the House; totals will keep moving as states count.
stories.why: From Jan. 3, Democrats will control what Congress votes on, its investigations and, in the Senate, confirmations for Trump’s last two years. Trump keeps his veto.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: Seat totals differ slightly between outlets because each uses its own race calls; this edition uses AP’s counts as published by the Guardian and says when it uses another desk.

stories.headline: Seven Senate flips, from Maine to Kansas to South Carolina
stories.glance: Seven GOP Senate seats flip, incl. Kansas and Texas
stories.deck: AP says Democrats took Republican-held seats in Kansas, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. Four sitting Republican senators lost.
stories.summary: In North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper beat Michael Whatley for an open seat, the first Democratic Senate win there since 2008, Ballotpedia notes; AP reported Cooper held a double-digit lead when the race was called. In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins conceded to Troy Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner as the Democratic nominee in July. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown beat Sen. Jon Husted in the special election for JD Vance’s old seat, a race AP says topped $500 million in spending. Josh Turek won Iowa’s open seat over Ashley Hinson; Adam Hamilton beat Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, which last elected a Democratic senator in 1932; and pediatrician Annie Andrews beat Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina. Ballotpedia says a seven-seat loss puts 2026 among its “wave” elections. Texas is covered separately.
stories.why: Democrats needed four pickups for a majority. Winning seven, several in states Trump carried easily in 2024, gives them room to spare.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Texas turns blue at the top: Talarico wins the Senate race and Hinojosa ousts Abbott
stories.glance: Texas: Talarico beats Paxton; Hinojosa ousts Abbott
stories.deck: Democrat James Talarico beat Attorney General Ken Paxton for the Senate, and Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott, who was seeking a record fourth term.
stories.summary: The Guardian reports the pair delivered the party’s first statewide wins in Texas since 1994: the last Democratic senator elected there was Lloyd Bentsen in 1988 and the last Democratic governor was Ann Richards in 1990. Talarico becomes the youngest member of the Senate and Hinojosa the state’s first Latina governor. ABC’s results showed Talarico at about 55% to Paxton’s 43% with roughly 97% of the expected vote counted. Talarico told CBS Mornings that his win sent a message to Elon Musk, who CBS says spent more than $150 million backing Paxton: “Texas is not for sale.” Down the ballot, Republican and former Yankees star Mark Teixeira won the open 21st District, the Guardian reports.
stories.why: Texas has 40 electoral votes and had not elected a Democrat statewide in three decades; both parties will read this as a test case for 2028.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Democrats hold Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire; El-Sayed becomes the first Muslim senator
stories.glance: Ossoff, El-Sayed and Pappas hold Democratic seats
stories.deck: Sen. Jon Ossoff won a second term in Georgia, Abdul El-Sayed beat Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan, and Rep. Chris Pappas beat former Sen. John Sununu in New Hampshire.
stories.summary: Ossoff, the only Democratic senator seeking reelection in a state Trump won in 2024, beat Rep. Mike Collins; AP coverage called it a blocked Republican target, and his victory speech called the results a rebuke of a “failed lame duck” president. El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, became the first Muslim elected to the Senate after a bitter race in which his primary rival, Haley Stevens, endorsed Rogers days before the vote, the BBC reports. Pappas kept Jeanne Shaheen’s open seat for Democrats; Sununu conceded, saying it was “not our night.” CBS News also projected Sen. Mark Warner reelected in Virginia and Peggy Flanagan winning in Minnesota. On the Republican side, CBS projected Sen. Pete Ricketts beat independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska.
stories.why: Republicans’ only realistic path to keeping the Senate ran through Georgia and Michigan; holding both meant Democratic gains elsewhere were pure upside.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Still uncalled: Alaska and Mississippi Senate races are on a knife-edge
stories.glance: Alaska and Mississippi Senate races still uncalled
stories.deck: In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola led Sen. Dan Sullivan by about 600 votes in AP’s count. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom led Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by a few dozen votes with about 96% counted.
stories.summary: AP figures shown by the Guardian on Wednesday morning had Peltola at 102,701 votes (48.2%) to Sullivan’s 102,075 (47.9%); neither race had been called. Alaska accepts overseas ballots for 15 days and does not run its ranked-choice tabulation until Nov. 18, which can swing results, the Alaska Current reports. The race was shadowed by a second candidate also named Daniel Sullivan; a Trump administration lawsuit seeking to block certification if the incumbent lost was dismissed by a federal judge on Sunday, CBS reports. In Mississippi, CBS rated the race a toss-up with only a few dozen votes separating the candidates. Neither result changes Senate control.
stories.why: These two seats decide whether Democrats finish at 54, 55 or 56 seats, and either could end in legal fights; leads are not wins.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: Donna Daily does not call races. Both are listed as uncalled by AP and as toss-ups by CBS News.

stories.headline: Democrats pass 218 in the House, with 68 races still counting
stories.glance: House: Democrats pass 218 (AP), 68 races left
stories.deck: AP says Democrats crossed the 218-seat majority line early Wednesday. Its tally at 9:10 AM ET: 228 Democrats, 139 Republicans and 68 races uncalled, many of them in slow-counting states such as California.
stories.summary: Ballotpedia counted 14 Republican House incumbents, and no Democrats, defeated as of 1:30 AM. Nine states redrew their maps mid-decade before this election, a push encouraged by Trump; Ballotpedia says the new lines should have helped Republicans by about nine seats, but if current leads hold Democrats will net about 15 seats across those states. AP’s live coverage says Democrats flipped districts Trump won by as much as 18 points in 2024. The Guardian’s live blog says the final Democratic total could reach 240 or more. Brooklyn’s Hakeem Jeffries is in line to become the first Black Speaker of the House.
stories.why: The House majority brings the speaker’s gavel, every committee chair and subpoena power, so expect investigations of the administration from January.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: House battlegrounds: Iowa flips three seats, Kean falls in New Jersey, Salazar and Boebert on the edge
stories.glance: Iowa flips 3 House seats; FL-27, CO-4 too close
stories.deck: Democrats won three of Iowa’s four House seats and ousted Rep. Tom Kean Jr. in New Jersey. In Miami, Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly leads; in Colorado, Rep. Lauren Boebert trails.
stories.summary: AP reported Christina Bohannan beat Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa’s 1st District, Sarah Trone Garriott beat Rep. Zach Nunn in the 3rd and Lindsay James won the open 2nd. In New Jersey’s 7th, Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett was projected to beat Kean, who called to congratulate her, ABC7 reports. In Florida’s 27th, Salazar led Democrat Eliott Rodriguez 50.27% to 49.73%, which NBC 6 says is a margin just wide enough to avoid a recount; Florida Politics reports Salazar has won, but Donna Daily has not seen an AP call. In Colorado’s 4th, Boebert trailed former Navy rear admiral Eileen Laubacher by about 1.5 points with more than 80% counted, the Guardian reports.
stories.why: These are the seats that show how far the wave reached into Trump country, and a few could still move as the last ballots are counted.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: FL-27 and CO-4 are described as leads only. NJ-7 is a network projection reported by ABC7.

stories.headline: Democrats flip governorships in Georgia, Texas, Ohio and Iowa, and win a majority of statehouses
stories.glance: Governors: Bottoms, Hinojosa, Acton, Sand flip states
stories.deck: AP says Keisha Lance Bottoms (Georgia), Gina Hinojosa (Texas), Amy Acton (Ohio) and Rob Sand (Iowa) won Republican-held governor’s offices. AP results at 9:10 AM ET: 28 Democratic governors to 20 Republicans, with two races uncalled.
stories.summary: Bottoms becomes the first Black woman elected governor of any state, AP reports; Acton beat Vivek Ramaswamy to become Ohio’s first woman governor, and Sand is Iowa’s first Democratic governor in two decades. The Guardian also lists Nevada as a Democratic pickup and reports Deb Haaland in New Mexico as the first Native American woman elected governor. ABC projects David Crowley will be Wisconsin’s first Black governor, and AP reports Sen. Amy Klobuchar won Minnesota’s governorship. Alaska’s race was uncalled, with Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins at 49.2% in AP’s count. In legislatures, Ballotpedia says Democrats flipped five chambers: the North Carolina House, both Wisconsin chambers, the Pennsylvania Senate and the Minnesota House.
stories.why: Governors and legislatures run elections, draw future district maps and decide on data centers and abortion. That power lasts well beyond 2028.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Ballot measures: abortion rights win in Missouri, Virginia and Nevada; Missouri voters scrap the GOP map
stories.glance: Abortion rights win; Missouri rejects GOP House map
stories.deck: Voters decided 145 ballot questions in more than three dozen states, AP reports. Abortion-rights supporters won in three states, and Missouri voters threw out a Republican-drawn congressional map.
stories.summary: Missouri voters defeated an amendment that would have brought back most abortion restrictions and banned some medical procedures for transgender minors. Virginia added a “fundamental right to reproductive freedom” to its constitution, and Nevada gave final approval to an abortion-rights amendment. Idaho voters rejected an abortion-rights law. In Missouri, voters also rejected the mid-decade map designed to win Republicans a Kansas City-area seat; Maryland approved an amendment that could allow new districts in 2028. Florida approved a major property-tax break for homeowners. California voters rejected a stricter voter-ID amendment, AP reports, while Ballotpedia counts citizenship-to-vote amendments passing in Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia, and voter-ID expansions in North Carolina and Ohio.
stories.why: Ballot measures go around legislatures. These results tell both parties where voters stand on abortion, election rules and redistricting.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: Ballotpedia’s 1:30 AM roundup still listed Nevada and Idaho as uncalled; AP’s 4:21 AM story reports both results.

stories.headline: California’s billionaire tax is too early to call
stories.glance: California billionaire tax: too early to call
stories.deck: AP says it is too early to call Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth.
stories.summary: The measure split California Democrats: progressives backed it, while Gov. Gavin Newsom and some party leaders warned it could drive the ultra-wealthy out of the state, the Guardian reports, and billionaires spent heavily against it. California routinely takes days to count: thousands of mail ballots are dropped off on Election Day, and in 2022 half the state’s votes were counted after Election Day, AP notes.
stories.why: It would be the first tax of its kind in the US. A win would push other states to try one; a loss would be cited against wealth taxes everywhere.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Hochul wins a second full term, beating Bruce Blakeman
stories.glance: Hochul re-elected New York governor
stories.deck: AP called the governor’s race for Kathy Hochul as polls closed at 9 PM. Republican Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive, conceded and called for unity.
stories.summary: Hochul led 63% to 37% with about 70% of the vote counted when AP called it, Gothamist reports, and took nearly 76% of the vote in New York City. She campaigned on energy rebate checks, a pause on data center construction and child care, and tied Blakeman to Trump at every turn. Her running mate, former City Council Speaker Adrienne Adams, will be the first Black woman to serve as New York’s lieutenant governor. Attorney General Letitia James was also re-elected, Al Jazeera reports.
stories.why: Hochul’s margin was far wider than her six-point win in 2022, and Albany now works with a friendlier Congress on federal funding for the state and the city.
stories.label: Reported

stories.dateLabel: Lawler conceded Tue night; count continues Wed
stories.headline: NY-17: Lawler concedes to Conley while Westchester counts ballots held back by a scanner glitch
stories.glance: NY-17: Lawler concedes to Conley
stories.deck: Republican Rep. Mike Lawler conceded to Democrat Cait Conley late Tuesday in the Hudson Valley’s 17th District. Westchester County began counting ballots Wednesday that its scanners could not read on Election Day.
stories.summary: The state Board of Elections said some Westchester machines missed a programming update, so ballots were sealed in emergency bags to be counted later; “Accuracy will never be sacrificed for speed,” it said. AP had not called the race when Lawler conceded around 11 PM, Gothamist reported, and ABC7 reported Wednesday morning that Conley had defeated Lawler as police escorted the ballots to the county board. NPR reports some right-wing commentators called the glitch fraud, while Lawler posted that “every ballot will be counted.” Elsewhere upstate, Gothamist reports Republican Anthony Constantino claimed victory in the open 21st District.
stories.why: This was one of the most expensive House races in the country and a top Democratic target since 2022. It is also a test of how a voting-machine glitch is handled under heavy scrutiny.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: Donna Daily has not seen an AP call in NY-17; the result rests on Lawler’s concession and ABC7’s report.

stories.headline: Brooklyn and NYC: Mamdani allies Lander, Valdez and Avila Chevalier head to Congress
stories.glance: NYC: Lander, Valdez, Avila Chevalier win House seats
stories.deck: CBS News projected wins for Brad Lander (NY-10), Claire Valdez (NY-7, parts of Brooklyn and Queens) and Darializa Avila Chevalier (NY-13), all backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
stories.summary: All three won safely Democratic seats after beating establishment candidates in June primaries: Valdez succeeds the retiring Nydia Velázquez, Avila Chevalier unseated Rep. Adriano Espaillat in the primary, and Lander beat Rep. Dan Goldman. Gothamist reports Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Grace Meng, Greg Meeks, Ritchie Torres and Hakeem Jeffries, who represents part of Brooklyn, won easily; Micah Lasher won the Manhattan seat of the retiring Jerry Nadler; and Republican Nicole Malliotakis held the Staten Island and southern Brooklyn seat. Nationally, Ballotpedia says candidates endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America won seven of their 10 House races, with three uncalled.
stories.why: New York City’s House delegation moves left, and a Brooklyn member, Jeffries, is set to run the House.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: NYC voters pass all five charter questions, including faster outdoor-dining permits
stories.glance: NYC passes all five charter ballot questions
stories.deck: According to unofficial Board of Elections results reported by amNY, all five questions from Mayor Mamdani’s Commission on Government Efficiency passed.
stories.summary: Question 1, which passed with 63.2%, removes mandatory public hearings for many private uses of sidewalks and the City Council’s power to reject individual sidewalk-café applications; the commission estimates outdoor-dining approvals could drop from as long as eight months to about two, starting March 1, 2027. Question 2 (61.6%) simplifies paperwork for city contracts, and Question 3 (65.5%) streamlines street-safety projects such as bike and bus lanes. Citizens Union and the Citizens Budget Commission backed Question 1; Common Cause New York opposed it, warning against cutting public input. Mamdani said New Yorkers “voted for a government that moves as fast as they do.”
stories.why: These changes affect daily city life: how fast restaurants can put out tables, how quickly bike lanes go in, and how the city signs contracts.
stories.label: Reported + official statement

stories.headline: Speaker Johnson won’t run for House GOP leader; Jordan and Scalise are eyed
stories.glance: Johnson won’t seek GOP leader post
stories.deck: Speaker Mike Johnson told staff Wednesday he will not run for minority leader in the new Congress, CBS and AP report, citing people familiar with the call.
stories.summary: House Republicans plan leadership elections on Nov. 10, CBS reports; ABC says candidates have until noon on Nov. 6 to declare. Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan are seen as likely contenders, and Fox News reported, per the Guardian, that Jordan is preparing a bid. Johnson had recently told CBS he intended to stay on as leader if Republicans lost the House. The BBC reports anger with Trump inside the party, with a top Texas Republican lobbyist calling the result “a total, complete rejection of President Trump.”
stories.why: Who leads House Republicans will shape whether the minority cooperates with or simply fights a Democratic House, including on spending deadlines.

stories.headline: Trump says he’ll accept the results, but blames candidates and warns of vetoes
stories.glance: Trump: “absolutely willing” to accept results
stories.deck: President Trump told the New York Times he was “absolutely willing” to accept the midterm results, NPR reports. He told Fox News the losses were not “a hit on me.”
stories.summary: In a Fox News phone interview, Trump said “the Democrats did a good job” and blamed Republican candidates rather than his policies, AP reports. He told CBS News that Democrats are “going to want to work with me. Otherwise I’d just veto everything.” The White House’s first Instagram post after the results read “PSA: TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT,” the Guardian reports. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called the night a “generational remake of the Senate map,” and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Americans “are crying out for transformational change.” NPR found no major disruptions at the polls despite fears of interference; Justice Department monitors were sent to every state.
stories.why: Trump accepting the result matters after months of fights over election rules. His veto threat is a preview of the next two years.
stories.label: Reported + official statement

stories.headline: What happens next: the last counts, the leadership races and Jan. 3
stories.glance: Next: Alaska count Nov 18; new Congress Jan 3
stories.deck: Most of what is still undecided comes down to slow counts in Alaska, Mississippi, California and a handful of House seats. The new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027.
stories.summary: Alaska waits for overseas ballots and runs its ranked-choice tabulation on Nov. 18. Mississippi’s Senate race is separated by a few dozen votes, and CBS calls it a toss-up. California routinely counts for days after Election Day, which is why many House seats there are still uncalled, AP says. In New York, Westchester began counting scanner-delayed ballots on Wednesday. House Republicans pick new leaders on Nov. 10. Under the 20th Amendment, the terms of the new House and Senate begin at noon on Jan. 3, when Democrats formally take control; until then, the current Republican majorities run the lame-duck session.
stories.why: The outgoing Republican majorities still run Congress until January, so any year-end deals happen before Democrats take over.
stories.label: Reported + official statement

stories.headline: A record early vote, near-record turnout, and voters angry about prices and the Iran war
stories.glance: Turnout ~49% (prelim.); 61M+ early ballots
stories.deck: More than 61 million ballots were cast before Election Day, 34% more than in 2022, NPR reports, citing the University of Florida’s Election Lab. Political scientist Michael McDonald estimates about 124.3 million people voted.
stories.summary: McDonald’s preliminary turnout rate of 49.42% of eligible voters would be the second-highest for a midterm since 1914, just below 2018’s 50.05%; he says it could move as California and Washington count mail ballots. In the AP Voter Poll, about six in 10 voters disapproved of Trump’s job performance, about 70% wanted Congress to check the presidency more, and about seven in 10 voters under 30 backed Democratic House candidates. CBS News exit polls found voters who called the economy bad backed Democrats, that men roughly split, and that Democrats’ lead with independents was decisive. Still, just over half of voters viewed the Democratic Party unfavorably.
stories.why: Big turnout and a broad swing suggest this was more a vote against Trump than a new love for Democrats, and the polls show both.
stories.label: Reported + analysis

stories.headline: Stocks jump while the dollar and Treasury yields slip after the sweep
stories.glance: Markets: Dow up ~2% at the open
stories.deck: The Dow rose more than 1,200 points, or 2.4%, shortly after Wednesday’s open, with the S&P 500 up 1.7% and the Nasdaq up 2.1%, CBS News reports. Stock futures had fallen overnight.
stories.summary: The Guardian’s business live blog reported the dollar down about 0.5% against major currencies, the 10-year Treasury yield down about 5 basis points to 4.91%, gold up 2.9% to $4,041 an ounce and Brent crude near $100.87 a barrel, about 2.7% lower. Defense stocks fell on expectations that the Pentagon’s $1.5 trillion budget request will face tougher scrutiny. Capital Economics told clients the result does not change much near-term because Democrats lack a filibuster-proof Senate and Trump can veto bills; other analysts said gridlock has historically been good for stocks.
stories.why: Markets are betting on gridlock, not big new laws. AI and data-center policy, and the Iran war, are what investors are watching.
stories.label: Reported + analysis

stories.headline: Abroad: Beijing calls it a “domestic affair”; Britain, Spain and South Africa react
stories.glance: China: midterms a “domestic affair”
stories.deck: China’s foreign ministry said the midterms are a US domestic matter and that Beijing is ready to keep working with Washington. Britain’s prime minister said the results were an “opportunity” for the world to focus on the cost of living.
stories.summary: Spokesperson Mao Ning, asked by the New York Times, said China would work with the US to “properly manage differences” and build a relationship of “strategic stability.” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said “President Trump has accepted the results” and called for ending the Iran war and fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the Guardian reports. RTHK, citing agencies, reports that French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said Trump still runs foreign policy and remains unpredictable, that Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said voters had rejected policies that “only impoverish,” and that South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the result would “introduce a new era in world relations.”
stories.why: Foreign governments know a president keeps control of foreign policy even when he loses Congress, so most of these reactions are cautious.
stories.label: Official statement + reported

stories.author: Donna Daily
stories.headline: A wave by any measure, but not yet a realignment
stories.glance: Our view: a wave, not yet a realignment
stories.deck: The scale is historic: seven Senate flips, Texas and Kansas, and a House majority decided in one night. Whether it lasts depends on things the result alone can’t tell us.
stories.summary: The case that this is a new era is strong. Ballotpedia says the seven-seat Senate swing puts 2026 among its wave years and notes the first time since 1954 that a party which won the Senate in one even year lost it in the next. AP’s Voter Poll shows young and Hispanic voters, who drifted toward Trump in 2024, swinging back hard. The case for caution is also real. Victor Davis Hanson points out that the White House party has lost House seats in about 90% of midterms since 1900, and that Clinton after 1994 and Obama after 2010 recovered. CBS exit polls show just over half of voters still view the Democratic Party unfavorably, and turnout, while high, was slightly below 2018’s. Our read: voters punished prices, the Iran war and corruption more than they embraced a Democratic program. What Democrats do with the gavels by 2028 will decide which reading proves right.
stories.why: The way this result is explained will shape what both parties do next, from primaries to the 2028 race.
stories.label: Our view

stories.author: Donna Daily
stories.headline: What a Democratic Congress can do, and what Trump’s veto still blocks
stories.glance: Our view: the limits of a Democratic Congress
stories.deck: A majority in both chambers gives Democrats the agenda, subpoenas and a check on nominations. It does not give them the votes to beat a veto or the Senate filibuster.
stories.summary: With the House, Democrats can open investigations, demand documents and testimony, and decide what comes to a vote; the Guardian lists Trump-family business, the Epstein files and Pentagon contracts as early targets. With the Senate, they can block or slow cabinet officials, ambassadors and judges. But 54 or so seats is short of the 60 needed to end most filibusters and far short of the two-thirds needed to override a veto, which Trump has promised to use. Democrats argue voters demanded “transformational change.” Trump argues they will have to deal with him or see everything vetoed, and markets are pricing in gridlock. Expect oversight and must-pass spending bills, not big new laws, to define 2027.
stories.why: It sets expectations. Most of what voters were promised will run into a veto, so watch hearings and budget fights.
stories.label: Our view

stories.author: Victor Davis Hanson
stories.headline: “Five lessons”: the biggest takeaway is how much we still don’t know
stories.deck: Hanson, a conservative historian, argues the losses fit a long pattern of midterm defeats for the White House party and may not derail Trump’s final two years.
stories.summary: Hanson notes that since 1900 the president’s party has lost House seats about 90% of the time and Senate seats about 75%, though he says Trump’s losses may rival Clinton’s in 1994 and Obama’s in 2010. Without a veto-proof Senate, he argues, Democrats will block judicial and cabinet nominees, but Trump will keep governing by executive order at home and acting largely as he likes abroad. His success, Hanson writes, will rest on the economy and on denuclearizing Iran, and quickly. Most of the column is behind a paywall; this summary covers the free portion.
stories.why: This is the strongest version of the argument that Tuesday was normal midterm gravity and not a verdict on Trumpism.
stories.label: Opinion

stories.author: Moira Donegan
stories.headline: “The death knell of Trumpism has finally sounded”
stories.deck: Donegan argues voters decisively curbed Trump’s power and that his 2024 win now looks like a reaction to inflation, not a lasting cultural realignment.
stories.summary: She writes that a Senate majority lets Democrats investigate the president and his cabinet, push their own agenda and block judicial appointments. She predicts Trump will alternately call the losses fake and blame others, but says such complaints are unlikely to go anywhere. Donegan blames gas prices driven by the Iran war and what she calls his frivolous, out-of-touch conduct, and expects ambitious younger Republicans to start turning on him as he enters 2027 with a hostile Congress and a term limit.
stories.why: This is a clear statement of the left’s view that the Trump era effectively ended on Tuesday night.
stories.label: Opinion

stories.author: Ben Davis
stories.headline: “Red and blue America have united” against Trump
stories.deck: Davis, a political data analyst who worked on Bernie Sanders’s 2020 campaign, argues that 2026 is not about one group or region swinging. He sees a rejection of Trump by every segment of the electorate.
stories.summary: Davis contrasts this year with recent elections that each had a single story, such as the 2018 suburban revolt or the 2022 backlash over abortion. He argues people tolerated Trump’s style in exchange for promised economic and physical security, and that his second term broke that bargain. Even the rosy polls, he says, missed the size of the wave. His conclusion: Trump has “depolarized” America, as truly red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina went blue.
stories.why: This data-focused argument is the opposite of Hanson’s “normal midterm” reading.
stories.label: Opinion
